earlier_scan.source_named: Calusa is extinct and known only from names/toponyms (Granberry 1994, Zamponi 2023 'Unclassified languages'); no phonological description exists

sources.citation: Ashrafyan, Konstantin. 2024. Calusa: The Lost Tribe of Florida (World Events and the Fate of the Disappeared Civilization Calusa and Their Neighbours). Self-published monograph; archive.org item book-calusa-hard-cover-difr-isbn-monograph-3-new-13082024-with-27-07-2024-lt-che (folkscanomy, open).
sources.note: no phonology content: the only language passages are 'The culture and language of the Calusa people presumably originated from the Tunica Indians..' (scanned line ~3598, p. ~257) and 'The Calusa language has little survival in speech, gestures, facial expressions, and sounds, although some research has been conducted in the 20th century' (line ~8241); a full-text search for stress/accent/syllable/tonal/phonolog/phonem/pronunc finds nothing linguistic.

sources.citation: Campbell, Lyle. 2024. Unclassified and Spurious Languages (chapter 5). In: The Indigenous Languages of the Americas: History and Classification, 280-338. Oxford: Oxford University Press. doi:10.1093/oso/9780197673461.003.0005
sources.note: nothing: 'known only from some place names and from about a dozen words reported in 1575'; 'extant record.. too scant to permit classification (Goddard 2005, 1, 11; Zamponi 2023, 1635-1636)'; no phonology

sources.citation: Campbell, Lyle. 2024. Unclassified and Spurious Languages. Chapter 5 of: The Indigenous Languages of the Americas: History and Classification, pp. 280-338. New York: Oxford University Press. DOI 10.1093/oso/9780197673461.003.0005.
sources.note: about a dozen words and place names; unclassifiable; no statement: nothing on stress, accent or tone anywhere in the chapter (the words stress/accent/tone/pitch/syllable do not occur); entry concerns attestation and classification only

sources.citation: Zamponi, Raoul. 2023. Unclassified languages. In Carmen Dagostino, Marianne Mithun & Keren Rice (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Indigenous North America: A Comprehensive Guide, Vol. 2 (The World of Linguistics 13.2), ch. 61, 1627-1648. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110712742-061
sources.note: read: entry = location, ethnohistory, whole surviving corpus (2-30 words); chapter has 0 tokens of stress/accent/pitch/prosody ('tone' only in 'stone'); no prosodic statement

sources.citation: Ferdinando, Peter. 2012. Review of Julian Granberry, The Calusa: Linguistic and Cultural Origins and Relationships (Tuscaloosa 2011). Florida Historical Quarterly 91(4): 584-586 (in 'Book Reviews', UCF STARS fhq/vol91/iss4/7; CORE mirror).
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone. Useful second-hand description of Granberry 2011: the linguistic part compares Calusa with other languages 'phonologically, morphologically, and semologically' (22) and 'will be familiar to readers of Granberry's 1995 paper on the Calusa language in The Florida Anthropologist' -- i.e. the 2011 book's phonology repeats the 1995 analysis (read here: no Calusa stress statement).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Calusa language' (accessed 2026-09-17), summarizing Granberry 2011 pp. 19-24 phonology and Zamponi 2024.
sources.note: Gives Granberry's reconstituted consonant/vowel inventory and corpus size ('a dozen words.. and 50 or 60 place names form the entire known corpus'); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Martin, Jack B. 2001 [draft dated 24 July 2001 of the chapter published as: Martin, Jack B. 2004. Languages. In Raymond D. Fogelson (ed.), Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 14: Southeast, 68-86. Washington, DC: Smithsonian Institution]. Southeastern Languages. PDF on author's site.
sources.note: nothing: 'The few words and place-names surviving in Fontaneda (1866) are unlike other southeastern languages.' No phonology. (The chapter's areal remark 'Many southeastern languages make use of pitch', draft p. ~44, names no target language and is not a statement about Calusa.)

sources.citation: Granberry, Julian. 1995. The Position of the Calusa Language in Florida Prehistory: A Working Hypothesis. The Florida Anthropologist 48(3): 156-173. Florida Anthropological Society. UF Digital Collections item UF00027829/00228.
sources.note: The only stress rule stated is Haas's for Tunica (p. 157: 'Tunica phonemes, as given by Haas (1946:337-341), are listed in Table 2.. Inherent stress occurs on the initial syllable of polysyllablic stems and on some affixes.'), immediately followed by 'Calusa phonemes, as reconstituted from Fontaneda's orthography in the present paper, are given in Table 3. Voiceless stops p, t, k, and ʔ were probably lenis and unaspirated' -- segments only. Tables 4-5 are 'Tunica-Calusa Stressed Vowel Correspondences' keyed to TUNICA stressed vowels. p. 162: 'There is insufficient data to say whether historic…

sources.citation: Sturtevant, William C. 1958. Accomplishments and Opportunities in Florida Indian Ethnology. In Charles H. Fairbanks (ed.), Florida Anthropology (Florida Anthropological Society Publications 5; Florida State University Notes in Anthropology 2), 15-55. Tallahassee. UF Digital Collections item AA00065677/00001.
sources.note: States that nothing of the language is known beyond a few names; no phonology of any kind.

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1922. Early History of the Creek Indians and Their Neighbors. Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 73. Washington: Government Printing Office. ['Calusa language' discussion pp. 28-31; Calusa town list pp. 331-333.]
sources.note: No phonology beyond incidental remarks: Guaragunve 'is almost the only one in which an r appears -- though Carlos is used for Calos occasionally'; 'In English the name would be pronounced nearly as Waragunwe'; Guasaca-esgui 'should probably be pronounced Wasaka-esgi'. Quotes Smith's Choctaw informants that the words 'are eminently Chahta in their sounds'. Nothing on stress, accent, prominence or tone.

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1917. Unclassified Languages of the Southeast. International Journal of American Linguistics 1(1): 47-49. doi:10.1086/463711.
sources.note: nothing: says only that 'we have scarcely any linguistic material from the South Florida tribes', that place names differ from Timucua and may point to a Muskhogean connection; no phonology, no stress/accent/tone anywhere in the article

sources.citation: Powell, John Wesley. 1891. Indian Linguistic Families of America North of Mexico. In Seventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1885-86, 1-142. Washington: Government Printing Office. [read in the Project Gutenberg plain-text edition, eBook 17286]
sources.note: Explicitly says no linguistic material of Calusa (or Tegesta) is available; only Fontaneda place-name terminations resembling Timuquanan names. No phonology, no prosody.

sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1884. A Migration Legend of the Creek Indians, with a Linguistic, Historic and Ethnographic Introduction. Vol. 1 (Brinton's Library of Aboriginal American Literature 4). Philadelphia: D. G. Brinton. [Section 'Calusa' pp. 13-15; remark on Fontaneda's 'seletega' under 'Seminole'.]
sources.note: No phonology. Only orthographic remark: 'The Spanish orthography, in which these names are laid down, is unfitted for transcribing Indian languages.. nevertheless, we recognize the frequently-occurring terminal -esta, -sta, which sounds quite like Timucua.' Under Seminole he reads seletega as Creek 'now pronounced silitiga, silitka'. Nothing on stress/accent/tone.

sources.citation: Smith, Buckingham (tr.). 1854. Letter of Hernando de Soto, and Memoir of Hernando de Escalante Fontaneda [c. 1575]. Washington. archive.org id letterofhernando00soto (scanned text).
sources.note: Nothing. This is the primary corpus (toponyms, chiefs' names, a dozen glossed words such as Zertepe, seletega); no remarks on accent or pronunciation apart from a note on the name Orizta.

sources.note: A linguist's 3-page assessment of Granberry's phonological and morphological analysis of the ~12-word + ~60-toponym Calusa corpus; whether it comments on prosody is unknown and, given the corpus, it almost certainly contains no tone statement beyond (possibly) remarking that suprasegmentals are unrecoverable. Listed only because it is the sole linguistic publication on Calusa not already listed here.
